question.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{x}^{2}-12x+8 & =-2({x}^{2}+6x-4) \\  & =-2({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+[{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}]-4) \\  & =-2({(x+3)}^{2}-13) \\  & =2(13-{(x+3)}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above in the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{22}{\sqrt{-2{x}^{2}-12x+18}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{22}{\sqrt{2(13-(x+3)^{2})}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{22}{\sqrt{26(1-(x+3)^{2}/13)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{22}{\sqrt{26}\cdot \sqrt{1-(x+3)^{2}/13)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{22}{\sqrt{26}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x+3)/\sqrt{13})^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse sine:

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(\frac{x+3}{\sqrt{13}}).$

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=\frac{x+3}{\sqrt{13}}.
$$

Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{13}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{22}{\sqrt{-2{x}^{2}-12x+18}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{22}{\sqrt{26}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x+3)/\sqrt{13})^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{22}{\sqrt{26}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{13}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{22}{\sqrt{2}}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =11\sqrt{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =11\sqrt{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{x+3}{\sqrt{13}})+C.\end{aligned}
$$
